stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Groundwater levels beneath the High Plains have been falling for decades, but not at the same rate everywhere. After mapping forty years of well records, ______ that the steepest declines cluster where irrigation wells sit less than a kilometer apart, a pattern suggesting that neighboring pumps draw down the same pocket of water faster than rainfall can refill it.
explanation: There is no article ('the' or 'a') before 'hydrologist,' so 'hydrologist Tomás Reyna' works as one label for the subject, and the name can't be fenced off. The subject 'hydrologist Tomás Reyna' then leads straight into its verb 'found,' and nothing should separate a subject from its verb. So you use no punctuation at all.

A.why: You treated the name as a removable appositive, as in 'my friend, Ana, said.' With no article before 'hydrologist,' the name is essential: if you remove it, you're left with 'hydrologist found,' which doesn't work. So the pair of commas is wrong.

C.why: You got the title and name right but put a comma after the name. That comma splits the subject 'hydrologist Tomás Reyna' from its verb 'found,' and nothing should come between them.

D.why: A colon has to follow a complete sentence. 'After mapping forty years of well records, hydrologist' isn't one, so the colon has nothing to introduce.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most self-healing polymers repair cracks only when they are heated, which limits their usefulness on bridges, ship hulls, and other surfaces exposed to cold air. A coating developed by ______ scratches at room temperature. Its surface is laced with microscopic capsules of liquid resin that burst when scraped, filling the gap and hardening within a few hours.
explanation: 'Materials scientist' has no article in front of it, so 'materials scientist Adaeze Okafor' is a single label and takes no internal punctuation. Now cross out 'developed by materials scientist Adaeze Okafor.' What's left is 'A coating seals scratches.' The verb 'seals' belongs to 'coating,' and no mark should come between that subject and its verb.

B.why: You put a comma between the title and the name, as if the name were an optional add-on. Without an article, the title and name form one label, so the comma breaks it apart. That comma also has no partner to close it.

C.why: The comma after the name sits between the subject 'A coating developed by…' and its verb 'seals.' One comma can't separate a subject from its verb, no matter how long the subject is.

D.why: A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas: it marks something you could remove. Here the name can't be removed, because 'developed by materials scientist seals' falls apart. So you shouldn't set it off with dashes.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Oakhaven's pocket parks—small plazas built on unused traffic islands, a strategy first proposed by ______ draw more weekday visitors than the city's largest park. City surveys suggest the reason is distance: nearly every resident now lives within a five-minute walk of one, while the large park lies at the edge of town.
explanation: This question has two steps. First, 'urban planner' has no article in front of it, so 'urban planner Lena Marchetti' takes no punctuation inside. Second, a dash after 'parks' opened an interruption much earlier, and it ends with the name. So it must close with a matching dash. Cross out the interruption and you get 'Oakhaven's pocket parks now draw more weekday visitors,' a complete sentence.

A.why: You noticed the interruption had to close but used a comma to close it. It opened with a dash, and the marks around an interruption have to match. A dash can't be paired with a comma.

B.why: The closing dash is right, but you added an appositive comma between the title and the name. With no article in front, 'urban planner Lena Marchetti' is one label and can't be split.

C.why: You correctly left the title and name unpunctuated but forgot the dash that opened after 'parks.' Without a closing dash, the interruption runs into the main verb, and the sentence no longer holds together.

stimulus: Rowers are often told that a long, static stretch before a race prevents injury and adds power. A.why: You used the appositive habit of putting a comma before the name. Without an article, the name is part of the label, so nothing goes between 'sports scientist' and 'Priya Natarajan.'

B.why: A single dash works like a colon, so it needs a complete sentence before it. 'Australian sports scientist' isn't a sentence. The dash also cuts the subject apart.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cover crops such as cereal rye can return nitrogen to depleted fields, yet farmers who plant them often report uneven results. Drawing on six seasons of plot trials, Iowa ______ identified the deciding factor: when the rye is killed off. Fields where it was terminated two weeks before planting consistently yielded more corn than fields where it was left growing until planting day.
explanation: 'Iowa agronomist' has no article in front of it, so 'Iowa agronomist Malik Osei' is a single label that serves as the subject. It runs straight into the verb 'has identified' with no punctuation. The colon belongs later in the sentence, after the complete clause that promises 'the deciding factor,' and not inside the subject.

A.why: You treated the name as a removable appositive. Take it out and you get 'Iowa agronomist has identified,' which needs an article to work. That shows the name is essential, so it can't be fenced off with commas.

B.why: The comma after 'Osei' comes between the subject and its verb 'has identified.' A single comma there splits the sentence's core in two.

C.why: You may have spotted that the sentence uses a colon and put one too early. A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and 'Drawing on six seasons of plot trials, Iowa agronomist' isn't one.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Beaver dams are usually studied for the ponds they create, but their effects downstream have received far less attention. In a three-year survey of mountain streams in northern Idaho, freshwater ecologist ______ found that stretches below active dams stayed cooler in late summer than comparable stretches without dams. She attributes the difference to groundwater that the ponds push into the surrounding soil, which later seeps back into the channel.
explanation: There is no article before "freshwater ecologist," so the title and the name work together as one label for the subject: "freshwater ecologist Maren Tillotson." That subject leads straight into its verb, "found," so you need no punctuation before the name and none after it.

A.why: You treated the name as an extra detail and fenced it off with a pair of commas. Without "the" or "a" before the title, the name is essential, so the commas cut one noun phrase in half.

B.why: You put a single comma after the name, which splits the subject "freshwater ecologist Maren Tillotson" from its verb "found." Nothing should come between them.

D.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and "In a three-year survey of mountain streams in northern Idaho, freshwater ecologist" is not one. The colon also breaks the title away from the name.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Researchers have long suspected that some songbirds raise their pitch to be heard over traffic noise. A 2021 study—designed by Brazilian ornithologist ______ recorded great kiskadees at forty sites around São Paulo. Birds singing near highways used notes that were, on average, about 200 hertz higher than those of birds in quiet city parks, a shift large enough to carry over the low rumble of engines.
explanation: This takes two steps. First, "Brazilian ornithologist" has no article, so it joins the name with no punctuation as a single label. Second, a dash before "designed" opened an interruption, and it has to close with a matching dash. Cross out "designed by Brazilian ornithologist Tomás Arruda" and you get "A 2021 study recorded great kiskadees," which is a complete sentence.

B.why: You closed the interruption with the right mark, but you also put a comma between the title and the name. With no article in front of "Brazilian ornithologist," the title and name form one unit and can't be split.

C.why: You kept the title and name together, but you forgot that the interruption opened with a dash. Opening with a dash and closing with a comma is a mismatch. Both ends of an interruption need the same mark.

D.why: You applied appositive commas around the name, which isn't right here because the name has no article in front of it. You also closed a dash-opened interruption with a comma, so the marks at the two ends don't match.

Their names for lagoons and sandbars often preserve shoreline positions that predate colonial surveys by more than a century, giving geographers a record of how the coast has shifted.

Inside the interruption, "Ghanaian cartographer" has no article, so the title runs straight into the name with no punctuation. Cross out the interruption and you get "A new atlas draws instead on the oral accounts," which is a complete sentence.

A.why: You closed the interruption correctly but also put a comma before the name, as if it were an appositive. With no article before "Ghanaian cartographer," the title and name are one label and take no comma between them.

C.why: You lost track of the comma after "atlas" that opened the interruption. Without a closing comma, the interruption never ends and runs right into the main verb "draws."

D.why: You saw that the interruption needed to close, but you used a dash for an interruption that opened with a comma. The marks at the two ends of an interruption have to match.

A.why: A colon has to come after a complete sentence. 'To avoid this problem, nutrition scientist' is a fragment, and the colon also cuts the subject's title off from the name it labels.

C.why: You applied the appositive-comma rule ('my friend, Ana, said'). With no article before 'nutrition scientist,' the name is essential and can't be set off by commas.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Eighteenth-century chamber music survives mostly in handwritten copies, and those copies rarely agree. A violin part made in Prague may carry trills that a Vienna copy of the same sonata leaves out. For years, scholars treated these differences as careless mistakes. In a 2019 survey of more than four hundred manuscripts, however, Czech musicologist ______ that copyists often changed ornaments on purpose so that the music suited the players in their own cities.
explanation: There is no 'the' or 'a' in front of 'Czech musicologist,' so the title and the name together work as a single label for the subject. That means no punctuation goes between the title and the name, and none goes between the name and the verb. The sentence also needs a conjugated main verb for its subject, and 'argued' provides it. 'Czech musicologist Radka Veselá argued that...' is correct.

A.why: You put a comma after the name. Nothing earlier in the sentence opens an interruption that this comma could close, so it just cuts the subject ('Czech musicologist Radka Veselá') off from its verb ('argued').

C.why: You treated the name as an appositive, as in 'my friend, Ana, said.' That only works when an article such as 'the' comes before the title. Without one, the name is essential, and commas around it break up a single noun phrase.

D.why: You got the punctuation right, but 'arguing' is a participle, not a main verb. The sentence ends up with a subject and nothing to say what that subject did, so it is a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Delivery apps often say that their couriers earn more than workers in comparable jobs. Those claims usually leave out the hours a courier spends waiting between orders. A 2021 report on app-based delivery in three Mexican cities, written by labor economist ______ that once waiting time was counted, median hourly pay fell by nearly a third. The finding has since shaped wage proposals in two state legislatures.
explanation: This takes two steps. First, cross out the interrupter. The comma after 'cities' opens the phrase 'written by labor economist...', and a second comma has to close it before the main verb. Without the interrupter, the sentence reads 'A 2021 report... found that...'. Second, 'labor economist' has no article in front of it, so nothing goes between the title and the name. The only choice that leaves 'labor economist Tomás Ibarra' intact and closes the interruption is 'Tomás Ibarra, found.'

A.why: You noticed that a closing comma was needed, but you also put a comma between 'labor economist' and the name. Without an article, the title and name form one phrase, so that first comma is wrong.

B.why: You followed the 'no comma after the name' habit and forgot that the comma after 'cities' opened an interruption. That interruption has to close before 'found', and without the closing comma the punctuation around it doesn't match.

D.why: You put the comma on the wrong side of the name. It splits 'labor economist' from 'Tomás Ibarra', and the interruption that began after 'cities' is still left open.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Some faults release stress without producing an earthquake anyone can feel. Over days or weeks, the rock on either side slides a few centimeters. Instruments register these slow-slip events, but people living above them notice nothing. After comparing two decades of GPS records from northern New Zealand, seismologist ______ that the events tend to recur at regular intervals, a pattern that could help forecasters judge when stress is building.
explanation: There is no article before 'seismologist', so the job title and the name work together as one label for the subject, and nothing should separate them. The opening phrase ('After comparing... New Zealand') is already closed by the comma before 'seismologist', so no other mark is needed before the verb. 'Seismologist Aroha Whitcombe proposed that...' is correct.

B.why: A semicolon has to join two complete sentences. Neither side qualifies here: 'After comparing... seismologist Aroha Whitcombe' has no verb, and 'proposed that...' has no subject.

C.why: You treated the name as an interruption that could be set off with a pair of dashes. A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas, and with no article in front of 'seismologist', the name is essential and can't be fenced off from its title.

D.why: You put a comma after the name as if it were closing an interruption, but no interruption was opened. The comma just separates the subject from its verb, 'proposed.'

C.why: You put a comma between the subject 'Chilean astrophysicist Marisol Quintero' and its verb 'counted.' A single comma should never separate a subject from its verb.
